design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.title: PCB Manufacturing and Assembly with Fusion and JLCPCB
design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.description:
This guide prepares a released Fusion Electronics design for fabrication and optional assembly. JLCPCB is a manufacturer to consider, not a course requirement. If you choose another service, use that manufacturer's current file formats, capabilities, and order rules.The standard course recommendation is a four-layer, 1.6 mm board with top-side assembly. A two-layer board can be a reasonable cost-saving choice. Your exported layers and order settings must match the board you actually designed; do not select four layers merely because an example did.Complete the design release review before generating the final package.Note The instructor checked the Gerber, placement, and BOM export paths below in their current Fusion version on 2026-10-08. Students use their own installations and are expected to keep Fusion up to date; menu labels may differ slightly between versions. Review the generated files and the manufacturer's upload preview for each design. Classify every component while selecting parts, not after routing:If using JLCPCB assembly, verify current stock, package, specifications, price, and service eligibility. An LCSC number in a library does not prove that the chosen part is correct or available. Preserve the manufacturer part number as well as the distributor/service identifier where practical.Prefer surface-mount devices (SMDs) when they meet the electrical and mechanical needs. Automated pick-and-place and reflow make ordinary SMD placement inexpensive. Plated through-hole (PTH) parts require manual insertion, hand soldering, or a separate wave-soldering process and can add substantial labor cost. Use PTH connectors or other parts when their mechanical advantages justify that cost, and consider whether the group should install them after delivery.JLCPCB classifies frequently used components as Basic parts and many other components as Extended parts. Basic and selected promotional/preferred Extended parts can avoid feeder-loading fees, while other Extended parts can add a per-part-type setup fee. Individual components can also carry minimum purchase quantities and additional attrition quantities for assembly loss. These categories, fees, minimums, and attrition allowances change; compare electrically acceptable candidates in the live parts library and review the actual quote rather than choosing from an old list.Top-side-only assembly is the course recommendation because it often reduces cost and complexity, but use the configuration that the design and selected service require.Keep the source revision and generated outputs together. A useful archive includes: schematic and PCB source revision; fabrication outputs and drill files; bill of materials (BOM); component placement list (CPL), also called pick-and-place or centroid data; assembly drawings or notes; DNP and group-assembled part lists; screenshots or exported reports from the final upload review; selected order settings and any approved substitutions. Regenerate all outputs from the same frozen revision. Do not mix a newer BOM with older Gerbers or placement data.Use Board Editor → Manufacturing → CAM Processor → Select Job → Process Job → ZIP file. Select an output job appropriate to the chosen manufacturer and stackup, then generate the ZIP containing the Gerber and drill outputs.Inspect the generated file list rather than assuming that a template fits the design. At minimum, the package normally represents: each copper layer actually used; top and bottom solder mask as applicable; top and bottom silkscreen as applicable; board profile or outline; plated and non-plated drill information as required; paste layers when the assembly or stencil process requires them. A two-layer design should not export fictitious inner copper layers. A four-layer design must include its two real inner layers with the intended ordering.Open the result in a Gerber viewer and inspect every layer, the outline, drills, mask openings, silkscreen, and alignment. The manufacturer's upload viewer is a second interpretation to review, not a replacement for checking local outputs.Use these export paths in the Board Editor: Placement data: Manufacturing → PickAndPlace → .mnt file → Edit Manually → CPL file. Preserve the raw export, then arrange its placement data into the supplier's CPL columns and save the final file as CSV. Changing the filename extension alone does not convert the file. Include the designator, X and Y coordinates, assembly side, and rotation; check each against the board. Bill of materials: Document → Bill of Materials → .csv file → Edit Manually → BOM file. Preserve the raw export, then arrange the columns for the supplier and add or verify exact part identifiers. Include only the intended vendor-assembled parts.
Check that the placement export includes every part intended for vendor assembly and that the final CPL identifies the correct side for each part. For a two-sided assembly order, include both sides in the same CPL. Preserve explicit and consistent units, and review the actual generated columns against JLCPCB's file-preparation guidance.For JLCPCB assembly, the BOM identifies what to place and the CPL identifies where and how to place it. Reference designators must agree exactly between them. JLCPCB's standard format uses millimeter coordinates and a layer/side field. ME5305 designs are normally laid out in mils in Fusion, so handle the conversion explicitly rather than allowing bare mil values to be interpreted as millimeters.Illustrative BOM structure:Comment,Designator,Footprint,LCSC Part # 10 kΩ,"R1,R2,R3,R4",0603,Cxxxxxx 100 nF,"C1,C2",0603,Cyyyyyy Illustrative CPL structure:Designator,Mid X,Mid Y,Layer,Rotation R1,38.100,38.608,Top,0 R2,40.640,38.608,Top,0 R3,43.180,38.608,Top,0 R4,45.720,38.608,Top,0 C1,25.400,43.180,Top,90 C2,27.940,43.180,Top,90 The example above uses millimeters. A course-tested alternative is to retain Fusion's mil coordinates and append the unit directly to every X and Y value:Designator,Mid X,Mid Y,Layer,Rotation R1,1500mil,1520mil,Top,0 R2,1600mil,1520mil,Top,0 R3,1700mil,1520mil,Top,0 R4,1800mil,1520mil,Top,0 C1,1000mil,1700mil,Top,90 C2,1100mil,1700mil,Top,90 Do not label bare mil values with millimeter headers. Whichever form you use, keep one coordinate unit throughout the file and verify the board scale, origin, and every component position in JLCPCB's upload preview.The BOM and both CPL examples describe the same six components. The part numbers above are placeholders, not recommendations. Quote a CSV field that contains commas. Validate that: every assembled designator appears once in the BOM and once in the CPL; letter case and spelling match; DNP and group-assembled parts are excluded or handled according to the service workflow; package and value match the selected part; units, origin, side, and rotation are consistent; no two different parts share one designator; the viewer places every component at the expected location and orientation. Fusion and the assembly service may use different rotation conventions or library origins. The uploaded placement preview is therefore a required design interpretation check, especially for IC pin one and polarized parts.Upload the fabrication package and choose settings that match the released design. Review layer count, thickness, copper weight, finish, solder-mask color, quantity, panelization, and any controlled-impedance or special-process options actually used.If ordering assembly: Select the intended assembly service and side or sides. Upload the BOM and CPL from the same release archive. Resolve unmatched or substituted parts by checking electrical specifications, package, orientation, lifecycle, and stock. Verify which parts are vendor assembled, group assembled, and DNP. Inspect every placement in the assembly viewer, not only the entries with warnings. Review board orientation, pin one, polarity, side, rotation, and omitted parts. Save evidence of the final configuration with the release archive. JLCPCB's current standard-assembly guidance includes service-specific edge-rail and fiducial rules. These rules can change and may depend on panelization or service type. Check the current requirements for the actual order instead of retaining a universal “two or three fiducials” or 1 mm component-edge rule. Source revision and all output files identify the same design. Fabrication layers match the selected stackup. Outline, drills, copper, mask, paste, and silkscreen render correctly. BOM and CPL designators reconcile exactly. Assembly scope distinguishes vendor-assembled, group-assembled, and DNP parts. Every selected part was checked for exact specifications and package. Placement side, origin, rotation, pin one, and polarity were inspected in the upload viewer. Order settings match the released board. Cost, quantity, shipping, and lead time were reviewed before purchase. The final package and review evidence were archived.
During manufacturing lead time, prepare the bring-up plan and firmware needed for initial tests.

design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.title: PCB Design Release Checklist
design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.description:
Design release is the decision to turn one identified PCB revision into manufacturing files. This checklist does not repeat the full schematic and layout guidance. It checks that the prior reviews apply to the revision being released and that later changes did not invalidate them.Completing a checklist does not guarantee that a board will work. The project group remains responsible for the release decision, including after peer and instructor feedback.Freeze this candidate while generating and reviewing outputs. If the schematic or board changes, create a new revision and repeat affected checks. Schematic review applies to this revision. Comments and unresolved questions from group and instructor review have recorded dispositions. Any schematic changes made during layout were re-reviewed. Schematic and PCB are synchronized. Each ERC finding has been resolved or approved with justification. DRC was run with rules appropriate to the selected manufacturer, and every violation has been corrected or deliberately justified. Peer and instructor review are important opportunities to find problems, but neither is certification that the design is ready to order. Exact manufacturer part numbers, values, ratings, and variants are identified. Symbol pins, footprint pads, package geometry, and pin-one conventions agree with the controlling documentation. Power sources, rails, expected loads, startup behavior, and thermal constraints remain valid. Required bypass, bulk, regulator, clock, reset, boot, interface, and protection components are present. Connector pinouts and viewing direction were checked against the real mating hardware. Intentionally unused pins and nets are documented. DNP and optional parts have explicit default states. Board outline, holes, slots, cutouts, and keepouts match the current mechanical design. Mounting hardware and tools clear copper and components. Connectors have mating and cable clearance in the assembled system. Critical current loops, return paths, power widths, copper areas, and thermal paths were reviewed. Copper pours were regenerated and checked for isolated islands, narrow necks, and lost connections. Exposed-pad and via-in-pad treatment matches part and assembly requirements. Test points, debug connector, controls, and indicators are physically accessible. A 1:1 print, mechanical model, or physical-fit check was used where it provides useful evidence. Each part is classified as vendor assembled, group assembled, or DNP. The assembly side and service match the board design. Component-to-edge, panel, rail, and fiducial decisions were checked against the selected manufacturer's current requirements. Pin one, polarity, connector orientation, board name, and revision are readable after assembly. Silkscreen does not overlap exposed pads or obscure assembly-critical markings. Likely rework areas remain accessible. The identified programming/debug tool and cable can connect to the board. Input, ground, and each regulated rail can be measured safely. Reset, boot, and recovery provisions are appropriate for the selected controller. High-risk subsystems can be isolated where the design calls for it. The first-power voltage, expected startup current, initial current limit, isolated loads, stop conditions, and first measurements are planned. Record remaining exceptions rather than making them disappear:The design is ready for CAM export when the group can explain the evidence for the current revision, the remaining risks, and the planned response if bring-up exposes a problem.
Continue with manufacturing and assembly file preparation.

design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.title: PCB Placement and Routing
design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.description:
PCB layout turns the schematic's logical connections into physical current paths. Placement determines whether those paths can be short, continuous, cool enough, accessible, and mechanically useful. Routing should therefore follow deliberate placement rather than repair an arbitrary arrangement of footprints.Start exploratory placement after the first coherent schematic blocks are built; do not wait for the entire schematic to accumulate into a large pile of unplaced parts. Work back and forth among schematic design, placement, and early routing. The board will often reveal packaging, connector, pin-allocation, and support-circuit changes. Keep the editors synchronized, and complete a schematic review before final routing and release.Before detailed placement, define: board outline and height limits; mounting holes, fasteners, standoffs, washers, and tool clearance; enclosure walls, panel openings, and mechanical keepouts; connector location, mating direction, cable bend radius, and insertion/removal access; buttons, indicators, sensors, antennas, and adjustment points that require exposure; expected assembly and rework methods; manufacturer capabilities and clearances for the selected service; layer arrangement, copper weight when relevant, and design rules. Print a 1:1 view when practical and compare it with real connectors, fasteners, and unusually large components. A correct footprint can still be unusable if a cable cannot be inserted or a screwdriver cannot reach a mounting screw.The standard course recommendation is a four-layer, 1.6 mm board with top-side assembly. A common starting arrangement is signal and components on the outer layers with an internal ground plane and an internal power or secondary routing layer. This is a recommendation, not a universal stackup.A two-layer board can reduce cost and may be reasonable for a simple design, but it usually requires more deliberate routing to preserve useful ground return paths. Students may choose reasonable settings for their project; course designs are limited to no more than four layers. Obtain the actual stackup and design rules from the selected manufacturer before final routing.Do not add internal copper layers to the manufacturing output unless the design actually uses them. The exported layer set must match the chosen stackup.For critical or unfamiliar parts, compare the placed footprint with the datasheet land pattern and package drawing. Check pad numbering, pitch, body outline, courtyard, pin one, exposed pads, holes, slots, and connector overhang.Do not treat Fusion's 3D rendering as the definitive footprint check. A plausible 3D body can be offset, incorrectly modeled, or associated with pads that do not match the real part. Within Fusion, the 2D board view is the best source for pad geometry, drill locations, outlines, and copper relationships. The final Gerber and drill outputs are the ultimate proof of what the manufacturer will fabricate, so inspect them before release.An exposed pad is not automatically ground. Its electrical connection, solder-paste pattern, thermal vias, and permitted via treatment come from the exact part and assembly process. Ordinary untreated via-in-pad can wick solder away from a joint; use it only when the land pattern and manufacturing process support it.Place components in this order, revisiting earlier decisions when needed: Place mechanically constrained parts: connectors, mounting holes, buttons, sensors, displays, antennas, and board-edge features. Place power entry, protection, regulators, and high-current loads so the main power path is direct. Place the microcontroller and other central devices with room for their required local support components. Place bypass capacitors, regulator components, oscillator parts, feedback networks, gate-drive loops, and other parts whose physical connection is electrically critical. Place remaining functional groups so their internal connections are compact and their interfaces face the appropriate neighboring blocks. Reserve readable silkscreen space for reference designators and functional annotations while adjusting component spacing and orientation. Reserve access for test points, programming cables, probes, and likely rework. Avoid clustering components merely because they belong to the same schematic sheet. The physical relationship that matters is the current path and return path.
Silkscreen needs physical space, so plan it during component placement rather than trying to fit every label after routing. Each populated part should have a legible reference designator that remains reasonably associated with that part after assembly. Also reserve space for the functional annotations selected in PCB Test Access and Rework.The standard Fusion/EAGLE convention is to print reference designators from the Names layer and not print component values from the Values layer. Values often become cluttered, may change without a footprint change, and are better recovered from the schematic and bill of materials. Show a value only when it provides a specific assembly or use benefit.This guide owns the physical space and layer decisions for silkscreen; the test-access guide owns the label content. Do not duplicate the same label in multiple forms merely because space is available.Current flows in a loop. A signal trace carries outgoing current, and copper elsewhere carries its return. At low frequencies the return may spread through available conductors; as edge rates increase, the return tends to follow near the signal path through the adjacent reference plane. Gaps, slots, or accidental plane splits can force a long detour and increase loop area, noise, and coupling.Mark the paths that deserve attention before routing: source through regulator and back to source; local bypass loop from capacitor to device supply and ground pins; switched-current loops in motor drivers, converters, and other power stages; clocks and other fast-edge signals; sensitive analog inputs and references; differential interfaces and their termination where applicable; high-current output and return paths. Keep a continuous reference under important signals. Group noisy and sensitive circuits through placement and return-path control; do not split ground automatically into “analog” and “digital” regions without a device-specific reason and a deliberate crossing strategy.This illustrative example uses the common 100 nF starting pattern. Use the value and number of capacitors required by the exact IC.Power plane/trace ───────┬──────── IC supply pin │ Cbypass │ Ground reference ───────┴──────── IC ground pin Place Cbypass so the supply-pin-to-capacitor-to-ground loop is short and direct. A schematic that draws all capacitors in one corner may still be electrically correct, but the PCB must place each local capacitor at the pin or supply group it serves. Do not move a bypass capacitor away from the pin merely to make probing easier; add a separate accessible test point.The PCB views below show local decoupling around an MCU, with C18 circled in the overview and enlarged in the detail. The capacitor and MCU ground pin use separate vias to the same nearby ground plane. The electrical sketch above does not prescribe a shared via; the physical placement preserves short connections and clearance for rework.
Figure MCU decoupling overview and close-up of 0402 capacitor C18. In the close-up, (1) is the MCU ground-pin return via and (2) is the capacitor return via, both connected to the continuous ground plane on the first internal layer (layer 2); (3) is the VDD supply connection from the second internal layer (layer 3). Route critical power and switched-current loops using widths, copper areas, and vias appropriate to current and temperature rise. Route clocks, sensitive analog nets, differential pairs, and other constrained signals according to their device requirements. Route remaining signals while preserving continuous return paths. Add and review planes or pours. Confirm that narrow necks, isolated islands, thermal reliefs, and antipads do not break intended connections. Add stitching vias where they serve a clear return-path, shielding, thermal, or structural purpose. Set trace width, clearance, via size, and copper-to-edge distance from electrical needs and the selected manufacturer's rules. A 6 mil signal trace is a common manufacturable starting point for ordinary low-current signals, but use wider traces when space permits and size power paths for their current and temperature rise. Ninety-degree corners are usually less important on these boards than continuity, clearance, manufacturability, current capacity, and return paths.In the first layout below, the input test points are tightly grouped beside the IC, and the output test points are squeezed between the IC and connector. The nearby electrolytic capacitor further limits probe approach. Electrical connectivity alone does not establish that the points will be usable during testing.
The improved layout moves the inputs to an accessible board edge and the outputs beside the connector, with a ground point in each group. The modeled oscilloscope probes and ground clip show the space needed to make simultaneous measurements. For a prototype, reserve enough space for planned measurements while keeping the increase in board area proportionate. Check access with the actual probes and connected cables, using a three-dimensional model where helpful. See probe access for selecting measurement points.
Figure Poor placement (first view) crowds test points around components; improved placement (second view) provides space for probes and nearby ground connections. Before release: Board outline, holes, cutouts, and keepouts match the mechanical design. Connectors, controls, indicators, and test points remain accessible in the assembled system. Footprints, pad numbers, pin one, polarity, and exposed-pad treatment match the exact parts. Critical current loops and return paths are short and intentional. Power widths and copper areas are supported by current and thermal estimates. Important signals do not cross reference-plane gaps without a planned return path. No required connection remains unrouted after pours are regenerated. Copper islands and narrow plane necks have been reviewed. Silkscreen does not obscure pads and remains readable after assembly. The design rule check (DRC) findings are fixed or documented as intentional exceptions. Schematic and PCB are synchronized. A 1:1 print or mechanical model has been checked where it adds useful evidence. DRC verifies declared geometric rules, not physical fit, current capacity, signal integrity, assembly orientation, or functionality.
The result is a routed board whose electrical paths, physical interfaces, and manufacturing assumptions can be explained. Continue planning test access and rework throughout layout, then use the release checklist on a specific revision.

design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.title: Schematic Design Workflow
design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.description:
A schematic is the electrical argument for your board. It should show what is connected, why each supporting part is present, and which assumptions must remain true for the circuit to work. Clear drawing matters because it makes the electrical argument easier to inspect, but a tidy schematic is not evidence that the circuit is correct.First-time designers need dependable starting patterns. This guide therefore gives standard choices that work well for many ME5305 projects, then identifies the checks needed before using them in a specific design. Start from the pattern; use the datasheet and project constraints to confirm it or modify it.Divide the system into functional blocks before selecting every symbol: power entry, protection, regulation, and distribution; microcontroller or other controller; sensors and analog signal conditioning; communication interfaces; output drivers, actuators, and external loads; programming, debugging, measurement, and recovery access. For each block, identify its inputs, outputs, supply rails, expected current, signal levels, and external connections. Confirm that the interfaces agree before drawing the detailed circuit. A 5 V output and a 3.3 V-only input, for example, require an explicit compatibility decision rather than a label added at the end.Consult assembly constraints early. Package availability, stock, assembly side, and hand-soldering plans can change part selection.Select the exact manufacturer part number, not merely a familiar family or package name. Similar suffixes may change voltage range, memory, pinout, temperature rating, or package.For every library component that can affect the design: Compare the symbol pin names and numbers with the device datasheet. Compare the footprint pad numbers and geometry with the recommended land pattern and package drawing. Confirm the symbol-to-footprint mapping. Check polarity and pin-one conventions. Check the physical mating view for connectors. Datasheets may show the plug, receptacle, top view, bottom view, or mating face. Mark intentionally unused pins with the CAD tool's no-connect mechanism when appropriate; do not leave their intent ambiguous. Verify copied blocks again in their new context. Reuse can preserve an old net name, value, or part variant just as easily as it preserves a good circuit.Use the exact device datasheet, reference manual, application notes, and a relevant reference design as a starting point. For a first design, the manufacturer's typical application circuit is usually the best initial pattern. Reproduce its required support circuitry, then check that its operating conditions match your source voltage, load, interface, and exact device variant.Trace power as a chain:source → protection and switching → regulation → distribution → loadsFor a low-voltage system powering an MCU, consider a low-dropout linear regulator (LDO) first. An LDO is often the simplest good choice when the input is only moderately above the output, the load current is modest, and the resulting power loss and temperature rise are acceptable. Consider a buck regulator when the voltage drop or load makes linear-regulator loss excessive, a boost regulator when the required rail is above the source, and a buck-boost regulator when the source may move above and below the required rail.Whichever topology you start with, check input range, output voltage, startup behavior, maximum and transient load, efficiency, power dissipation, thermal path, noise, and required external components.Document each rail before completing the circuit:Distinguish four capacitor roles: Local bypass capacitors supply short transient currents near device power pins. Bulk capacitance supports a rail over longer load changes and interconnect impedance. Regulator input and output capacitors may be required for stability and transient response. Special supply-pin capacitors support internal regulators, references, or analog domains. As a starting pattern, place a 100 nF (0.1 µF) ceramic bypass capacitor at each IC power pin or power-pin group. This is appropriate for many ordinary digital ICs and gives first-time designers a useful default. Then check the datasheet: an IC may call for a different value, multiple capacitor values, separate treatment for analog or internal-regulator pins, or a capacitor for each individual supply pin. Also verify dielectric, voltage rating, and any effective-capacitance concerns.
Schematic grouping helps reviewers see which capacitor serves which pin. The schematic position does not create electrical proximity; the short, low-inductance physical connection is established later in the PCB layout.If USB, a battery, and a bench supply can power the board, decide how to prevent unintended backfeeding and how the sources will be selected. Simple diode isolation, a power multiplexer, or an ideal-diode circuit may be appropriate depending on allowable voltage drop, current, cost, and source behavior. This choice matters only when the design actually has interacting power sources. Label input-voltage limits where a user can see them.Begin an MCU circuit with this standard support checklist: connect every supply pin and supply domain, with the local bypassing recommended above; provide an accessible hardware programming/debug interface; give reset a defined default state and consider a reset button or test point; determine whether the internal oscillator is sufficient or an external crystal/oscillator is useful for the required timing accuracy and interfaces; confirm the default boot mode and consider a jumper, solder bridge, or test pad when alternate boot access would improve recovery; include any special capacitors or connections required for internal regulators, analog supplies, references, or backup domains. Reset pull resistors, external crystals, and boot-selection hardware are common and often good choices. Confirm their values and connections for the exact MCU rather than copying them unchanged from another design.ME5305 lab hardware includes ST-Link modules detached from Nucleo-L476RG boards. These provide a six-pin Serial Wire Debug (SWD) connection and a UART-to-USB bridge. Plan a compatible, accessible hardware-debug connection; verify the lab cable's pinout, the target-voltage reference behavior, ground, SWDIO, SWCLK, and any reset connection before assigning a board header. Do not treat a pin labeled VDD or target voltage as a general programmer power output without checking the hardware documentation.
A bootloader can provide a firmware-programming path, but it does not replace source-level hardware debugging. Whether boot-mode access is useful depends on the MCU and the recovery strategy. See programming and recovery.For every interface, verify voltage levels, logic thresholds, direction, idle state, required bias, drive capability, and protection at external connectors. UART transmit connects to the other device's receive. Label direction from a clear point of view. Each ordinary SPI peripheral generally needs an independently controlled chip-select signal, with a defined inactive state. I²C pull-up resistance depends on bus capacitance, permitted rise time, supply voltage, and device sink-current limits. Multiple pull-ups act in parallel; they do not electrically “contend,” but the combined resistance may be too low. Name active-low signals consistently and check their meaning against the datasheet truth table. A common course convention is the N prefix, such as NRESET. Fusion can display an overbar when a name is enclosed in exclamation points, for example !RESET!. A suffix such as RESET_N is also understandable; consistency matters more than the selected convention. Floating inputs require an intentional default state unless the device documentation permits them to remain open. Check output current, voltage, switching transients, and the safe state during reset. Size LED resistors rather than copying a familiar value. Add flyback, gate-drive, snubber, current-limiting, level-shifting, electrostatic-discharge, or transient protection when the connected device and environment require it.Group related circuits, use descriptive net names, and make signal flow easy to follow. A left-to-right signal flow with power above and ground below often helps, but clarity is the goal rather than a rigid drawing rule.Schematic position and wire shape normally communicate logical organization, not PCB position, trace length, or routing. Drawing two parts next to one another does not cause Fusion to place them together on the board. When a physical relationship is important—such as placing a bypass capacitor beside a supply pin, keeping an oscillator loop compact, or locating a connector at a board edge—state it with an explicit schematic note and enforce it in the PCB layout.Show reference designators, values, and relevant ratings. Useful annotations include tolerance, voltage rating, dielectric, power rating, inductor current rating, crystal frequency, LED color, connector mating part, and default jumper population. Avoid long wires when net labels communicate the connection more clearly.Functional blocks may occupy separate sheets or clearly identified regions. Keep the schematic readable without requiring a reviewer to guess which local labels are connected or which side of a connector is shown.The electrical rule check (ERC) compares connections with pin and net types declared by the part libraries. It can reveal useful problems such as unconnected pins, conflicting outputs, and missing power declarations. In Fusion and its EAGLE-derived libraries, it can also flag connections that are electrically intentional because the library metadata does not describe the circuit well.Run ERC and examine each finding. Resolve a real problem, or approve the finding with a short justification when the circuit is intentional. The goal is an understood ERC report, not necessarily a report with no warnings. ERC is a supplemental review tool; it is less important in this workflow than datasheet-based schematic review and the PCB design rule check (DRC).Synchronize the schematic and PCB after every change.Begin exploratory PCB placement once the main functional blocks, exact parts, and their connections are established. You do not need to wait until the schematic is perfectly reviewed: moving between the schematic and board editors helps you build one subcircuit at a time instead of accumulating dozens of unplaced parts. Placement and early routing will often expose pin-allocation, footprint, connector, or support-circuit changes that belong back in the schematic.
The work is a repeated dance among schematic design, placement, and routing. Keep the two editors synchronized, and complete the schematic review before final routing and design release.

design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.title: Schematic Review Checklist
design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.description:
Review the schematic by tracing how the system must behave, not by glancing at a completed drawing. Layout may already be underway; the goal is to identify unresolved design questions before final routing and release make them expensive to change.This checklist assumes that the design decisions are explained in the schematic workflow. When a check fails, return to the owning explanation rather than inventing a rule at review time.Identify the exact design revision and record unresolved items. This can be a short project note rather than a separate formal submission.Begin at each possible source and trace to every load. Input connector pinout, polarity, voltage range, and current capability match the real source. Protection, switching, fusing, and source-selection behavior are intentional. Multiple sources cannot backfeed one another or an external host unexpectedly. Every regulator is suitable for its input range, load, loss, thermal conditions, and startup behavior. Regulator input/output components match the exact device documentation. Every device power pin and special supply domain reaches the correct rail. Each ordinary IC power pin or power-pin group begins with the 100 nF bypass pattern unless its datasheet supports a different choice. Bulk, regulator, analog-domain, internal-regulator, and other special-pin capacitors match the exact device requirements. Rail names and units are consistent throughout the design. Expected rail loads and voltage ratings have reasonable margin. Ask what the circuit does during connection, startup, steady operation, shutdown, and an incorrectly connected source. Manufacturer part numbers identify the intended variants. Symbol pin numbers match the datasheets. Footprint pad numbers and package dimensions match the selected parts. Polarized parts and pin-one conventions are unambiguous. Connector numbering was checked from the correct viewing direction and against the mating hardware. Component values, units, tolerances, ratings, and relevant attributes are present. Reused circuit blocks were rechecked in this design. Intentionally unused pins follow the device guidance and are explicitly marked. Reset, enable, and boot signals have defined startup states. Active-low signals are named and interpreted consistently, using a clear convention such as NRESET or Fusion's !RESET! overbar notation. Clock components and values match the selected clock source and device guidance. A working programming/debug connection is included and compatible with the intended tool. Recovery provisions are appropriate for the selected MCU; they are not copied from another family without verification. Firmware pin assignments agree with the schematic. For the lab's detached Nucleo-L476RG ST-Link modules, verify the actual six-pin SWD cable and target-voltage-reference behavior rather than relying on a generic online header drawing. Logic levels and thresholds are compatible at every interface. UART direction, SPI chip selects, I²C pull-ups, and other bus requirements are correct. Pull-up and pull-down networks produce the intended effective resistance and default state. Outputs can drive their loads under normal and transient conditions. Inductive loads have an intentional current-decay path where required. External interfaces include suitable current limiting, level translation, and protection where the environment requires it. LED polarity and resistor sizing are correct. Functional blocks and signal flow can be followed without guessing. Important nets have descriptive, consistent names. Reference designators and values are assigned. Each ERC finding has been resolved or approved with a short justification. Schematic and PCB are synchronized after the latest change. Remaining questions are written down with a person responsible for resolving each one. An ERC report is supporting evidence, not functional verification. Fusion's library metadata can produce warnings for intentional circuits, while a clean report can still miss a mirrored connector, wrong part variant, unsuitable regulator, or misunderstood datasheet.Members of the project group are expected to check one another's work. Each group will also have a short in-person PCB review with the instructor, and additional feedback may occur through email or Piazza.Treat every review as another opportunity to find issues, not as sign-off. The instructor will not state that a design is guaranteed to work or is ready to order. Reviewers can miss things, and any design can be improved. The group remains responsible for resolving comments, verifying the final revision, and deciding when to release it.Record comments and their disposition:
The review is complete when unresolved items are visible and owned, not when every checkbox has been made to look clean. Continue the placement-and-routing process with the reviewed revision, and repeat the affected checks whenever the board-layout dance leads to a schematic change.

design-guides/schematic-and-pcb-design-g.description:
These guides support the path from a project concept to a manufactured and tested printed circuit board. They assume that you understand basic circuits but may have little PCB-design experience. Your component datasheets, project constraints, and selected manufacturer's current requirements remain the controlling sources for a particular design.A checklist cannot prove that a board will work. Use these guides to expose assumptions, collect evidence, and decide what must be checked next.The sequence follows the main hardware-realization stages, but the work is iterative. Treat schematic design, placement, and routing as a repeated dance: build a coherent subcircuit, place and begin routing it, then return to the schematic when the board exposes a better pin assignment, package, connector, or support circuit. Plan programming and measurement access throughout, consult assembly constraints before committing to packages, and keep the schematic and board synchronized.Board construction is also a design choice. A four-layer, 1.6 mm board with top-side assembly is the standard course recommendation, and JLCPCB is one manufacturer to consider. A two-layer board may be a reasonable cost-saving choice. Choose settings that fit the project and manufacturer; course designs are limited to no more than four layers. Design the schematic. Establish the architecture, select exact parts, add required support circuits, and review the electrical rule check.
Review the schematic. Trace the design systematically and record unresolved questions before final routing and design release.
Place and route the PCB. Translate the schematic into a board that satisfies electrical, mechanical, assembly, and fabrication constraints.
Plan test access and rework. Make the board practical to program, measure, isolate, understand, and repair.
Review the design for release. Confirm that one specific revision is ready to become a manufacturing package.
Prepare and review manufacturing files. Generate fabrication and assembly outputs, reconcile them, and inspect the uploaded interpretation before ordering.
Bring up the assembled board. Apply power under controlled conditions and validate the hardware from power rails outward. The result from each stage should be carried into the next one: a reviewed schematic, a routed board, a release revision, a manufacturing archive, and finally a bring-up record.
Adding silkscreen artwork is optional enrichment. Functional labels, polarity marks, connector identification, and board revision information take priority over artwork.Project-group members are expected to check one another's work. The instructor will conduct a short PCB review with each group and may offer more feedback in person, by email, or through Piazza. This feedback is advisory, not a certification that a design will work or is ready to order. PCB design always admits further improvement, and your group remains responsible for verifying and releasing its design.

topics/bldc-motors/hall-effect-sensors-e.title: Hall-Effect Sensors, Encoders, and Commutation
topics/bldc-motors/hall-effect-sensors-e.description:
Commutation is the process of changing the stator excitation as the rotor turns so that current continues to produce torque in the desired direction. A brushless motor requires electronic commutation because it has no mechanical commutator.Table Three useful levels of commutation, in order of increasing complexity. The ME5305 core path emphasizes Hall-sensored six-step commutation and driver selection. Sinusoidal commutation and FOC are included so students can recognize the terms and evaluate whether a driver IC provides them.Many small motors contain three digital Hall-effect switches. Their outputs change as rotor poles pass the sensors. With appropriate placement, the three signals divide an electrical revolution into six sectors of electrical each. The Hall signals identify a sector rather than the exact rotor angle within that sector.The example below uses the same angle datum as the motor model: when the rotor permanent-magnet field is aligned with the positive phase- magnetic axis, and positive is counterclockwise. Sector 1 is centered on this datum and extends from to electrical. The remaining sectors follow in increments.Three binary Hall signals permit eight codes, but only six normally occur in a correctly operating six-sector sequence. Codes 000 and 111 are commonly treated as invalid. For increasing , the mapping used in the figure is001 → 101 → 100 → 110 → 010 → 011 → repeat Only one Hall bit changes at each ideal sector boundary. Decreasing traverses the codes in the opposite order. This mapping is only an example: actual Hall order and polarity depend on sensor placement, connector pinout, phase wiring, and direction of rotation. Use the motor documentation or determine the mapping experimentally at low energy.Figure Example three-Hall sequence for increasing electrical angle . The dotted boundaries divide one electrical revolution into six sectors. The code written above each sector is ordered as . Only one ideal Hall channel changes at each boundary; the mapping is motor- and wiring-dependent, and reverse rotation traverses the codes in the opposite order. In six-step commutation, two phases are intentionally driven while the third phase is left floating. Define the ideal leg-state commandwhere requests that phase be connected toward the positive DC bus, requests that phase be connected toward the DC return, and requests a high-impedance state in which neither switch in that leg is intentionally on. Here is an abstract command state, not necessarily the voltage on one physical MCU pin. A particular motor driver may encode these three states with two logic inputs, a PWM input plus an enable input, a serial command, or internal Hall-commutation logic. Even when , winding current may temporarily establish a phase voltage through body-diode conduction or synchronous freewheeling.
The signal names and STM32-aligned timer terms used below are collected in the short index.With the established back-EMF convention, the following ideal sequence produces positive torque for increasing . At a sector boundary, the half-open intervals assign the boundary to the sector on its right; is equivalent to in the next electrical revolution.Table Hall sensor commutation lookup table.
Figure Example Hall-sensored six-step commutation sequence for positive torque and increasing electrical angle. The datum matches the motor and back-EMF model: the rotor permanent-magnet field is aligned with the positive phase- magnetic axis. Each Hall code identifies a electrical sector. The ideal commands , , and request the high-side, low-side, and high-impedance leg states, respectively. In the winding diagrams, black windings carry the idealized driven current and gray windings are floating; the arrows show the actual conduction direction rather than redefining the positive phase-current references. The rotor arrow represents at the center of each sector. The rotor drawings use one pole pair for clarity; in general, , so the six-sector sequence repeats times per mechanical revolution. High-frequency PWM, dead time, current ripple, and driver-specific freewheel paths are omitted. The table defines one internally consistent Hall and phase-excitation mapping, not a universal lookup table. To implement six-step commutation on an unfamiliar motor, associate each observed Hall code with the appropriate driven phase pair and verify the result at low energy. Reversing the desired torque while holding rotor position fixed swaps the high and low commands for the two active phases. Reversing the direction of rotor motion causes the measured Hall codes to occur in the reverse order.
Figure Ideal tri-state phase commands for the example six-step sequence. The levels show the requested sector states; PWM, dead time, and current recirculation are omitted. Within each ideal sector, current enters the motor through the phase commanded high, passes through that phase winding to the conceptual neutral point, and leaves through the winding of the phase commanded low. The third phase is not intentionally driven. The bottom two rows of Figure 2 pair this current path with the rotor orientation at the center of the sector. Under the selected conventions, the resulting stator excitation continues to pull the rotor in the positive direction as increases.Actual winding current does not change instantaneously at a sector boundary. Inductance, back-EMF, PWM, dead time, and the selected freewheel strategy determine how current transfers between phases. Figures 2 and 4 therefore show the ideal commanded path used to understand the sequence, not every instantaneous semiconductor-conduction state.
Figure Ideal winding-current path in each six-step sector. Black windings are intentionally driven, gray windings are floating, and arrows show conventional current from the phase connected toward the positive DC bus to the phase connected toward the DC return.
Figure Rotor permanent-magnet orientation at the center of each electrical sector for the one-pole-pair illustration. The corresponding stator current pattern produces positive torque as the rotor advances from left to right. Torque or speed is commonly adjusted by applying PWM to one of the active legs, or by using a driver-specific recirculation pattern. The exact strategy changes current ripple, switching loss, braking behavior, and current-sense visibility. The implementation developed below applies PWM to the phase whose abstract state is and uses the low-side zero state for synchronous slow decay.
Figure Animated relationship among phase excitation, the resultant stator field, and rotor orientation during one electrical revolution of ideal six-step commutation. Each 1.5-second frame shows the center of one sector. The two driven phase-field components combine into the labeled resultant stator field, which advances in steps and remains ahead of the rotor permanent-magnet field for positive torque under the selected conventions. The and symbols show the positive-current reference directions into and out of the page for the and conductors. Figures 2 and 5 provide static views of the same sector sequence. The block-commutation table describes each phase with the abstract state . The microcontroller must translate that three-state request into timer settings and binary logic signals that the assumed gate-driver interface can accept. Figure 7 shows this signal flow using STM32-aligned timer terminology. It is a feedforward signal-flow diagram rather than a feedback-control diagram; the physical dependence of the Hall signals on rotor position is not drawn as a return path.
Figure Signal flow for Hall-sensored block commutation using synchronous slow decay and STM32-aligned timer terminology. The Hall code and direction command select the abstract states , , and . Firmware maps those states and the duty request into the driver enables and timer compare values . The three PWM channels share the timer count , auto-reload value , and prescaler . Each binary output enters a gate driver that inserts dead time before producing and . Power connections, protection and fault handling, current sensing, and device-specific configuration interfaces are omitted. For the active-high PWM convention used here, the timer output is high while . The exact endpoint behavior and register scaling depend on the selected microcontroller timer, but the conceptual state mapping is:Table Truth table decoding the tri-state abstract state into binary and signals. The assumed driver then interprets and as follows:Table Truth table decoding the binary and signals into inverter-leg behavior. Here means that the input is ignored. When and changes, the gate driver temporarily requests both switches off to insert dead time. Actual gate-source voltages have finite propagation and transition times, so the MOSFET conduction state does not change instantaneously with the logic input.In sector 6, Hall code 011 selectsThe timer and driver command mapping is thereforeThe phase- driver input is the PWM waveform, is ignored because phase is disabled, and continuously requests the phase- low-side state. When , the inverter applies the motoring state and drives current from phase to phase . When , phases and are both commanded low, giving the zero state used for synchronous slow decay. Phase remains floating throughout the sector.This example fixes one decay strategy so that the signal path is explicit. Other drivers or applications may use a high-impedance interval, diode freewheeling, high-side recirculation, or a different input encoding. Follow the selected driver data sheet when converting the abstract states into physical input signals.Figure 8 extends the same mapping across three consecutive sectors at a constant duty request. The PWM waveform moves from phase in sector 4 to phase in sectors 5 and 6 because the phase commanded by changes with the commutation table. At each boundary, the enable pattern changes so that the newly floating phase is disabled and the two active phases implement the next driven current path.
Figure Physical driver-interface signals for sectors 4, 5, and 6 using synchronous slow decay and a constant duty request . The Hall code and abstract state tuple above each sector come from the six-step table. A phase with has and a PWM waveform on ; a phase with has and ; and a phase with has , making its shaded value a don't-care condition. Only a few PWM cycles are drawn per sector for legibility; in normal operation, the PWM frequency is much higher than the electrical commutation frequency. Before driving an unfamiliar motor at full bus voltage: Confirm phase-to-phase winding continuity and isolation from the frame. Rotate the shaft slowly and record the Hall-code sequence in both directions. Verify that only six valid codes occur and that only one Hall bit changes at each boundary. Identify the phase order and connect it to the driver's expected order. Use a current-limited supply and a low command while checking direction, current, and temperature. Stop if the rotor locks, chatters, reverses unexpectedly, or draws excessive current; those symptoms often indicate a phase/Hall mapping error. An incremental encoder commonly provides quadrature channels and , plus an optional index channel . The phase relationship between and gives direction, and counted edges give relative position.An incremental encoder does not automatically provide absolute rotor electrical angle at power-up. A controller may need an index search, a known alignment pulse, stored calibration, or additional absolute information before applying high-performance commutation. Mechanical encoder angle must also be converted to electrical angle and corrected for the offset between encoder zero and the rotor magnetic axis:The offset is a calibrated quantity whose sign depends on the selected angle convention.A resolver uses an excited winding and two approximately sinusoidal output channels to encode shaft angle. Interface electronics excite the carrier, condition and demodulate the returned signals, and estimate angle. Dedicated resolver-to-digital converters are common because the raw signals are not logic-level sine and cosine values that can simply be connected to a microcontroller.Magnetic and optical absolute encoders can also report shaft angle directly. Regardless of sensor technology, a commutation system must know resolution, latency, direction, pole-pair count, and the electrical-zero offset.Sinusoidal commutation commands three smooth phase waveforms displaced by electrical. Space-vector PWM (SVPWM) is another way to synthesize the requested three-phase average voltage from the same inverter. The detailed switching-vector hexagon and dwell-time derivation are intentionally deferred from the core notes.In a center-aligned implementation, the desired sinusoidal phase commands can be represented as compare-register trajectories centered on . The timer still produces binary waveforms by comparing its rapidly varying value with these slowly varying compare values; the smooth curves in Figure 9 are therefore duty commands, not motor-terminal voltages or phase currents.
Figure Example sinusoidal compare-register commands , , and over one electrical revolution. The three commands are separated by electrical and centered on . In the figure, denotes their normalized modulation depth, so the extrema are and . FOC uses the measured electrical angle to express the measured phase currents in coordinates that rotate with the rotor. For the surface-PMSM operating region emphasized here, the direct-axis current command is normally , while the quadrature-axis command sets the requested torque. Separate current controllers produce the rotating-frame voltage commands and , which are transformed back into three-phase voltage commands for the PWM inverter.
Figure High-level inner current-control loop for surface-PMSM FOC. The - and -axis PI controllers regulate and and produce the voltage commands and . The inverse Park/Clarke transform uses the measured electrical angle to form the stationary three-phase command . The sensing path illustrates phase-current measurement using shunt resistors, a programmable-gain amplifier (PGA), an analog-to-digital converter (ADC), and current reconstruction before the measured currents are transformed into . The rotor-position path measures shaft angle and applies the pole-pair count and calibrated offset so that . A resolver or other position sensor could replace the encoder-based path, while a sensorless estimator would infer electrical angle from available electrical measurements and the motor model. Detailed current-controller decoupling, voltage saturation, anti-windup, field weakening, maximum-torque-per-ampere control, and PWM switching are omitted. Figure 10 begins with the current commands and therefore does not show an outer speed or position loop. The command may be calculated directly from a requested torque or supplied by an outer speed controller; a position controller may in turn surround the speed loop. These outer loops change how is generated, but they do not change the basic inner current-loop structure shown here. The illustrated current-sensing chain is also representative rather than universal: a particular motor driver may measure all three phase currents, reconstruct one or more currents from fewer shunts, or integrate some of the amplification and conversion circuitry.For a small mechatronic system, ask: Does the motor already include Hall sensors or an encoder? Does the driver accept those signals directly, or must the microcontroller decode them? Is position needed only for commutation, or also for mechanism feedback? Is valid absolute angle required immediately at startup? Does the sensor resolution support the selected commutation method and speed range? Are logic levels, pullups, cable shielding, filtering, and connector pinout compatible? How will direction, pole-pair count, and electrical-zero offset be calibrated and verified?

topics/bldc-motors/motor-theory-fundamen.description:
Scope and terminology In these notes, BLDC motor means the broad class of brushless permanent-magnet synchronous motors with approximately sinusoidal back-EMF. Some vendors reserve BLDC for trapezoidal-back-EMF machines and use PMSM for sinusoidal machines. Always check the manufacturer's terminology. This note develops only the physical ideas needed to interpret a small brushless motor and its driver: flux linkage, back-EMF, electromagnetic torque, and the relationship between electrical and mechanical angle. A detailed electromagnetic field derivation is outside the scope of this module.The naming convention and notation style used throughout this lecture series are collected in the index.Begin with a stationary coil and a permanent-magnet rotor. The rotor field links the coil differently as the rotor turns. That changing flux linkage produces a voltage at the coil terminals.
Figure Cross-sectional view of a simplified one-phase permanent-magnet motor. The and symbols indicate current directed into and out of the page, respectively. For positive , current enters the page at and leaves the page at . By the right-hand rule, the positive magnetic axis of the winding points along the positive -axis shown in the figure. Rotor orientation is defined by the counterclockwise electrical angle , measured from the positive -axis to the idealized permanent-magnet field vector . The figure assumes one pole pair (), so ; in general, . Magnetic flux linkage, , measures how strongly magnetic flux links all turns of a winding. In the idealized motor, assume that the rotor magnet produces a sinusoidal permanent-magnet flux linkage in phase :where is the peak permanent-magnet flux linkage of one phase.
Figure Idealized permanent-magnet flux linkage versus rotor electrical angle. In the idealized one-phase motor, the permanent-magnet field is assumed to have constant magnitude and a uniform spatial distribution while its direction rotates with the rotor. Consequently, the flux linkage of phase varies sinusoidally with electrical angle . The permanent-magnet back-EMF is the time derivative of the permanent-magnet flux linkage when the phase-voltage polarity is defined as the drop from the positive terminal to the negative terminal :Applying the chain rule giveswhere is electrical angular speed. The negative sign is a consequence of the selected angle, terminal polarity, and flux-linkage definitions.
Figure Idealized phase- back-EMF versus rotor electrical angle at constant speed. For constant positive electrical speed , the back-EMF follows : it is zero when the rotor field is aligned with the phase- axis and reaches its peak magnitude one-quarter electrical revolution later. Ignoring losses, the instantaneous electrical power converted to mechanical power by one phase isFor the one-pole-pair model, , soPositive average torque therefore requires the phase current to be synchronized with rotor position. For example, with the sign convention above, choosewhere is the peak phase current. This current produces nonnegative instantaneous torque:A practical motor uses three displaced windings so that their combined torque is much smoother than the torque from this one-phase thought experiment.The main derivation assumes one rotor pole pair:For a motor with pole pairs, the general relationship isThe one-pole-pair assumption keeps the geometry readable, but it must not be carried into a real motor's speed or commutation calculations without checking the motor pole count.A phase-peak back-EMF constant referenced to mechanical speed can be introduced throughBecause and ,Therefore, for the one-pole-pair model used in the main derivation. A manufacturer's reported value may differ numerically if it uses line-to-line rather than phase voltage, RMS rather than peak voltage, or a speed unit other than radians per second.The torque constant similarly depends on how current is defined. Do not assume two numerical constants are directly comparable until all of the following are known: phase or line-to-line voltage, peak, RMS, or average voltage, mechanical or electrical angular speed, phase, line, peak, or RMS current, and SI units or a vendor-specific speed constant such as rpm/V. Rotor motion changes permanent-magnet flux linkage and therefore produces back-EMF. Back-EMF magnitude increases with speed. Torque depends on both current magnitude and current alignment with the rotor field. Electrical angle advances by one revolution per pole pair for each mechanical revolution. Sign and scaling conventions are choices, but every equation, plot, sensor mapping, and driver connection must use the same choices.

topics/bldc-motors/three-phase-inverters.description:
A three-phase inverter connects a DC source to the three motor terminals with three half bridges. By controlling the six semiconductor switches, the inverter establishes phase-current direction and magnitude. A monolithic motor-driver IC may integrate only the gate drivers, or it may integrate the gate drivers, power transistors, current sensing, commutation logic, and control loops.Each motor terminal is connected to the midpoint of one half bridge. The high-side switch connects that terminal toward the positive DC bus; the low-side switch connects it toward the negative DC bus. Modern small-motor drivers normally use MOSFETs, either integrated in the IC or connected externally.Figure Simplified three-phase inverter power stage with six N-channel MOSFETs, their body diodes, three low-side current-shunt resistors , and a wye-connected motor. The dashed boundaries distinguish the DC bus, power stage, current-sense elements, and motor. The pole potentials , , and , the floating neutral potential , and the sense nodes are all referenced to GND.
